title: Perplexity-directed prefetch and early-exit: MoE case study across long-context Llama/Mistral/Qwen
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a set of exploratory experiments and profiling notes for a small, targeted optimization: using per-request perplexity estimates to drive two complementary runtime behaviors for MoE-style models on long context workloads: (1) adaptive KV prefetching priority (which experts/kv shards to warm earlier) and (2) heuristic early-exit from expert compute for low-surprise tokens. The goal is to reduce end-to-end tail latency and GPU load without materially degrading quality for Llama, Mistral, and Qwen families when serving long-context requests (> 8k tokens) with mixed MoE and dense layers.

Why this came up: many long-context traces show large portions of the request that are low-surprise (highly predictable continuation) after the prefix. In MoE routing scenarios we see disproportionate expert fanout during unpredictable windows and low utilization otherwise; naive prefetch of all candidate experts and uniform compute allocation increases latency and GPU memory pressure.

High-level idea:
- Compute a lightweight perplexity proxy at A/B router entry (cheap ngram or small transformer head) on the first N tokens of each request or on sliding windows.
- Use the proxy to:
  * Rank experts/kv-shards for prefetch order (high perplexity => warm more experts aggressively).
  * Permit early-exit or skip expert tails when the perplexity falls below a tunable threshold (skip expensive FFN/experts and substitute a cached dense estimate or short-circuit projection).

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Models: Llama-2-13B-MoE (internal patch), Mistral-MoE-7B variant, Qwen-MoE-14B prototype. Dense baselines included standard Llama-2-13B/dense and Mistral-7B/dense for control.
- Context lengths: 4k, 8k, 16k (tokenized via runtime tokenizer used in production).
- Workloads: 1) conversational (system prompt + back-and-forth), 2) doc-append (long static doc + query), 3) streaming token generation (server-side streaming, 32 token chunks).
- Routing policies: top-1 deterministic, top-2 stochastic, balanced-gating with capacity factor 1.2.
- Prefetch strategies compared: no-prefetch, naive all-candidates, perplexity-ranked partial-prefetch (top N where N derived from perplexity percentile), sliding-window dynamic.
- Early-exit thresholds: none, ppx_proxy < 3.0, ppx_proxy < 2.0.

Key measurements and probes collected per request:
- end-to-end latency (p50/p90/p99), token-level generation latency, GPU SM utilization, GPU memory overcommit events, kernel launch counts for expert kernels, KV prefetch latency and miss rate, quality delta (self-BLEU/next-token cross-entropy vs baseline).
- Profiling hooks used: per-kernel timestamps + NVTX, per-request KV cache hit telemetry, router-vs-expert breakdown in traces.

Results (summary):
- Latency: the perplexity-ranked partial-prefetch + early-exit at ppx<3.0 reduced p95 end-to-end latency by 18-26% on average across models at 8k context for the conversational workload. Gains larger (22-30%) on doc-append where large low-surprise tails existed. p99 improvement was smaller (8-12%) because tail spikes often driven by network jitter and cold-starts not solved by prefetch alone.
- Throughput: tokens/s increased modestly (6-12%) due to reduced kernel launch churn when early-exit triggered.
- GPU utilization: SM occupancy smoother (fewer short bursts) leading to ~10% reduction in average GPU power draw during long-serving windows.
- KV prefetch bandwidth: total prefetched KV bytes down by 35% relative to naive all-candidates — prefetch prioritized hot experts and avoided cold shards for low-ppx windows.
- Quality: measurable but small quality deltas. For threshold ppx<3.0, next-token cross-entropy increased by 0.02 nats on average (within noise for many workloads). Self-BLEU/ROUGE on downstream extractive tasks showed <1.5% delta. For aggressive threshold ppx<2.0, quality drift became noticeable for creative/ambiguous prompts.

Model-specific observations:
- Llama-MoE: Continues to benefit the most from expert-prioritized prefetch because router tends to produce compact expert sets; prefetching the top-2 based on perplexity ranking captured the majority of hot fanout. Early-exit worked well when prefix was instruction-heavy.
- Mistral-MoE: Router is more diffused — perplexity ranking still helps but required top-4 prefetch to match quality. Early-exit was less frequent for Mistral (deduced from proxy), but when triggered it produced larger latency gains because Mistral's expert FFNs are comparatively heavier per token.
- Qwen-MoE: Showed sensitivity to the proxy design; Qwen's tokenization and longer subtoken spans meant our ngram proxy under-estimated surprise for certain inputs. Re-tuning proxy window length solved most of this.

Side-effect and risk notes: 
- Proxy cost: running the proxy itself adds CPU work; we implemented a tiny transformer head compiled to CUDA for hotspot workloads and a fallback ngram estimator on CPU for low-throughput paths. Proxy adds 0.4-0.9ms median overhead but saves 6-18ms in tail-heavy traces.
- Cold-starts: If requests arrive cold without warm KV caches, perplexity ranking helps little since warmup must still fetch core KV shards; mitigation: combine perplexity with a small 'always-warm' expert set for cold-starts (observed best is top-1 always-warm + perplexity-ranked for the rest).
- Monitoring & alerting: quality regressions are subtle. We need a continuous eval with prompt-level slicing (creative vs deterministic prompts) to ensure early-exit isn't silently harming important user classes.

Profiling snapshots (selected numbers, 8k context conversational, p95 improvements):
- Baseline (naive prefetch, no early-exit): p50 86ms, p95 243ms, p99 460ms, kernel launches per request 14, prefetched KV 1.0GB
- Perplexity-ranked partial-prefetch (top N dynamic): p50 84ms, p95 198ms, p99 420ms, kernel launches 10, prefetched KV 0.68GB
- Perplexity-ranked + early-exit (ppx<3.0): p50 80ms, p95 179ms, p99 408ms, kernel launches 8, prefetched KV 0.61GB, quality delta +0.02 nats

Implementation notes (runtime):
- Router hook: added an async estimate phase that races with tokenization. If estimate completes before routing decision commit, runtime annotates the router decision with a ppx score and prefetch priority flags. If not, fallback to policy-based default.
- Prefetch queue: prioritized queue that runs on a separate prefetch worker pool with soft deadlines tied to chunk emission. Eviction policy updated to prefer keeping top-1 always-warm experts across requests.
- Early-exit: implemented as a conditional path in the expert execution pipeline; when triggered, we short-circuit to a light linear projection + layernorm substitute computed from cached dense statistics for that position to avoid the heavy FFN kernel. This path is instrumented and reversible (we can recompute offline for evaluation).
- Safety: guarded by feature flags and per-customer rollout gating. We saw customer-specific workloads (legal docs with highly uniform phrasing) where this produced large wins with zero quality loss.

Open follow-ups / next experiments: 
- Better proxy models: test a distilled 20M-head proxy trained to predict model surprisal across the three families. Hypothesis: ~30% better gating precision, fewer false early-exits.
- Quant-aware prefetch: integrate quantization profile into expert ranking (some experts cheaper when quantized).
- Adaptive thresholds per-customer and per-route (learned via low-signal bandit).
- Offline recompute pipeline: periodically recompute outputs for early-exit traces to surface any rare regressions and feed into an automated rollback trigger.

Action items (short):
- [OWNED: Connor] Build the 20M distilled proxy training job (JIRA-RT-1902).
- [OWNED: Diego] Add per-route feature flagging and metrics (JIRA-RT-1895).
- [OWNED: Aisha] Prepare canary rollout plan for Dedicated pools (timeline: 3 weeks).

Notes to reviewers:
- These are early experiments; results vary by workload and router topology. The perf wins look promising for typical long-doc workloads and for conversational tails where predictability increases as the session evolves.
- Please look at the linked PR for the runtime changes; kernel-level instrumentation is verbose — trusting Connor to pare down before final merge.

Slack threads: #perf-moe, #prod-deploy (see pinned links in linked_artifacts).

Appendix: quick glossary and heuristics tried:
- ppx_proxy: our lightweight estimator for per-window perplexity; tuned window sizes: 16/64/256 subtokens.
- top-N prefetch: choose smallest N such that cumulative router probability mass > f(perplexity), where f is a monotonic mapping we tuned via grid search (linear and log variants).
- always-warm: a small set of experts (1 or 2) kept resident to reduce cold-start pain.

End of doc. Will iterate after the 20M proxy runs complete.
